common_name: Houma Pecan (Desirable x Curtis Scab-Resistant Gulf Coast Pecan)

planting.note: Plant a dormant bare-root or container-grown grafted tree in late winter into deep, fertile, well-drained bottomland-type soil; pair with a cultivar of the opposite pollen-shed type for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with room to develop into a large shade tree, and site a compatible pollinizer nearby since pecans are wind-pollinated and set a heavier crop with cross-pollination. Houma was developed by USDA-ARS breeder L. D. Romberg at Brownwood, Texas from a controlled cross of Desirable and Curtis, and it carries good-to-moderate scab resistance that makes it noticeably more forgiving than Desirable alone in the humid Gulf South. Nuts run about 55 per pound with roughly 51% kernel and bright, attractive golden kernels, though trees can be susceptible to downy spot and early fall freezes. Water deeply during nut fill in late summer and apply a spring foliar zinc spray, since pecans are heavy zinc feeders on Gulf Coast soils.
sources: USDA-ARS Pecan Genetics and Breeding Program — Pecan Cultivars: Houma

planting.note: Plant a dormant grafted tree in late winter into deep, well-drained soil; Owens is a Type I (protandrous) pollen shedder, so pair it with a Type II cultivar such as Stuart, Elliott, or Kanza for full cross-pollination.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and site a Type II pollinizer nearby, since Owens sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive. Long recommended for the Mississippi Delta and Arkansas, Owens is prized mainly for its reliable scab resistance and tree health rather than top nut quality: nuts are large and thick-shelled with moderate, fairly consistent production, which makes it most valuable as a dependable yard pollinizer alongside a higher-quality cultivar. Its Type I bloom habit and pest tolerance keep it productive in humid Southeastern summers with less fungicide input than scab-susceptible standards. Apply a spring foliar zinc spray and water deeply during nut fill in late summer, as pecans are notoriously heavy zinc feeders.

common_name: AU Buck I Chestnut (Auburn University Blight-Resistant Chinese Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU Buck I is an early-season selection in the AU Buck succession-bearing series developed at Auburn University's Chinese chestnut breeding program, and like other Chinese chestnuts it needs a second, genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct Chinese chestnut cultivars for cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Buck I is among the earliest-dropping cultivars in Auburn University's AU Buck series, bred specifically to extend wildlife food-plot nut drop from late summer onward. Like other Chinese chestnut selections it carries strong natural resistance to chestnut blight, the bark canker disease that eliminated American chestnut from Eastern forests, and it begins bearing within a few years of planting rather than the decade or more typical of seedling trees. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy and good air circulation, which helps limit fungal disease pressure during humid Deep South summers, and collect nuts promptly from the ground as the spiny burrs split open in fall.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct Chinese chestnut cultivars for cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; AU Buck III is a mid-season selection that drops nuts over a 4-5 week period beginning about late September, developed at Auburn University's Chinese chestnut breeding program, and like other Chinese chestnuts it needs a second, genetically distinct cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant two or more genetically distinct Chinese chestnut cultivars for cross-pollination in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. AU Buck III is a precocious, heavy annual bearer with nuts averaging about 10.9 grams that begin dropping around late September and continue for four to five weeks. common_name: Hare Black Walnut (Illinois Large-Nutted Black Walnut)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree while dormant in deep, well-drained soil well away from vegetable beds and other juglone-sensitive plants; Hare is late-blooming, which helps it dodge late-spring frosts that can damage earlier-flowering black walnuts.

directions: Hare is an Illinois-origin black walnut selection grown for a large, smooth nut with good shell structure that gives a notably high first-crack and total kernel percentage for the species. Its late bloom time is an advantage in regions prone to late frost, since flowers emerge after the risk of damaging cold has largely passed. Plant a grafted tree in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from tomatoes, blueberries, and other plants sensitive to the juglone black walnut roots release into the soil, and give it the wide mature spacing the species requires. Harvest nuts promptly after they drop and hull them quickly to avoid staining and mold.

common_name: Snyder Black Walnut (New York Named Black Walnut Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree while dormant in deep, well-drained soil away from juglone-sensitive garden plants; Snyder has performed well in nut-evaluation trials across New York and Ohio.

directions: Snyder is a named black walnut selection out of New York valued for plump, well-colored nuts that have scored well in regional nut-evaluation trials across New York and Ohio. Grafted trees bear sooner and more predictably than seedling black walnuts, though like most black walnuts the kernels still require patient cracking. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, siting it well away from tomatoes, apples, and other juglone-sensitive plants, since black walnut roots release a growth-inhibiting compound into the surrounding soil. Allow the wide mature spacing the species needs and collect dropped nuts promptly, hulling them quickly to prevent staining.

common_name: Beck Black Walnut (Spur-Type Named Black Walnut Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree while dormant in deep, well-drained soil away from juglone-sensitive garden plants; Beck's spur-type growth habit produces more bearing wood along the branches than typical black walnuts.

directions: Beck is a named black walnut selection distinguished by a spur-type growth habit, bearing nuts on short spurs along the branches rather than only at shoot tips, which tends to concentrate production. In nut-evaluation trials it has averaged roughly 16 grams per nut with a kernel percentage in the high-20s, typical for the species. Plant a grafted tree in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping it well away from tomatoes, apples, and other juglone-sensitive plants, since black walnut roots release a growth-inhibiting compound into the soil. Give it ample mature spacing and collect dropped nuts promptly, hulling them quickly to prevent staining and kernel discoloration.

common_name: Lake English Walnut (Self-Fertile Cold-Hardy Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained loam; Lake is self-fertile and can be grown alone, though yields improve with a second cold-hardy Persian walnut cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Lake is a self-fertile, cold-hardy Carpathian-type Persian walnut suited to home orchards in colder regions than the thin-shelled California cultivars typically tolerate. Nuts ripen in early fall, falling free of the husk when mature, and crack easily from a thin shell to release a mild, sweet kernel. Plant in deep, well-drained loam in full sun, giving the tree room to mature into a broad, shade-casting specimen that can take four to five years to bear a first meaningful crop. While self-fertile, planting a second compatible Persian walnut cultivar nearby improves nut set and yield.

common_name: Chico Walnut (Early-Season UC Davis Persian Walnut Pollenizer)

planting.note: Plant a bare-root grafted tree in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile loam; Chico leafs out and harvests earlier than most Persian walnut cultivars, so it is most often grown as a pollenizer alongside a main-crop cultivar.

directions: Chico is a University of California walnut selection notable for its early-to-midseason harvest, used commercially mainly as a pollenizer for later-blooming cultivars since its pollen shed overlaps well with their female bloom. Nuts are smaller than main-crop cultivars like Chandler but crack cleanly with good kernel color. Plant in deep, well-drained loam in full sun, and pair it with a compatible main-crop Persian walnut if the goal is a dependable kernel harvest rather than pollination support alone. Expect a broad, vigorous canopy at maturity, so allow generous spacing from buildings and other trees.

common_name: Ashley Walnut (Early-Harvest Heritage California Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant a bare-root grafted tree in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile loam; Ashley is an early-harvest heritage California cultivar, self-fertile but more productive with a compatible second Persian walnut cultivar nearby.

directions: Ashley is a heritage California Persian walnut cultivar grown for its early harvest and large, attractive, light-colored kernels. It is self-fertile and can bear a crop on its own, though older orchard records note it can be an inconsistent, alternate-bearing producer compared to later commercial standards. Plant in deep, well-drained loam in full sun, allowing room for a broad, spreading mature canopy, and water deeply through summer nut fill since walnuts are not drought tolerant. Harvest as soon as the husks begin to split in early fall to preserve kernel color and flavor.

common_name: Felix Hazelnut (OSU Eastern Filbert Blight-Resistant Pollinizer)

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, well-drained loam in full sun; Felix is grown primarily as a pollinizer for Jefferson and Dorris, so plant it within pollination range of those or other compatible main-crop cultivars.

directions: Felix is an Oregon State University hazelnut release bred for strong resistance to eastern filbert blight, used primarily as a pollinizer whose bloom timing complements main-crop cultivars like Jefferson and Dorris. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, siting it within pollination range of the main-crop trees it is meant to support, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and self-incompatible. Harvest begins once nuts drop free of the husk in early fall; collect promptly from the ground to limit mold and losses to squirrels and jays.

common_name: PollyO Hazelnut (High-Yield OSU Filbert Blight-Resistant Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, well-drained loam in full sun; plant a compatible pollinizer nearby, since hazelnuts are self-incompatible.

directions: PollyO is an Oregon State University hazelnut release combining a high level of resistance to eastern filbert blight with vigorous growth and heavy yields. Nuts are small to medium with a high kernel percentage, good kernel quality, and an early maturity date that allows harvest ahead of many other cultivars. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible blight-resistant pollinizer nearby, since hazelnuts will not set a crop alone. Harvest once nuts drop free of the husk in early fall, gathering promptly from the ground to reduce mold and losses to wildlife.

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in deep, well-drained loam in full sun; Clark carries quantitative (partial, multi-gene) resistance to eastern filbert blight rather than the single dominant Gasaway gene, giving it value as blight pressure shifts to new strains.

directions: Clark is an Oregon State University hazelnut selection valued for quantitative resistance to eastern filbert blight, expressed as shorter cankers and good overall vigor rather than complete immunity from a single resistance gene. This broader-based resistance has taken on added importance as new eastern filbert blight strains have begun overcoming the Gasaway gene relied on by many older blight-resistant cultivars. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer nearby, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and self-incompatible. Harvest once nuts drop free of the husk in early fall, collecting promptly from the ground to limit mold and losses to squirrels.
